speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: asked the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (a) whether guidelines on managing heat stress at workplaces are regularly updated to incorporate the latest scientific evidence; and (b) whether these guidelines will consider any preliminary findings of the Third National Climate Change Study.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: And for any supplementary questions to Question Nos 1 to 4 to be taken after the reply to Question No 7 has been given, as the issues raised in Question Nos 1 to 7 are inter-related and will be addressed jointly by myself and the Senior Minister of State for National Development Tan Kiat How.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I will address them together with Senior Minister of State Tan Kiat How in two parts.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: First, I will set out the broad context of how climate change and rising temperatures will affect Singapore and outline the Government's approach to strengthening Singapore's heat resilience.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Senior Minister of State Tan Kiat How will then elaborate on specific policies and measures to cool our neighbourhoods and community spaces.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In recent weeks, many countries have been experiencing heatwaves, including China, India, Pakistan and many European countries.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Record-breaking temperatures above 40 degrees Celsius have resulted in deaths, heat injuries and damaged infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: These heat waves are increasing in frequency and intensity worldwide as a result of climate change and portends the severe consequences we would face if we do not take significant steps today to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, as well as to mitigate and adapt to the impacts of climate change.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Singapore will not be spared from the impacts of global warming – 2012 to 2021 was our warmest decade on record.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This is compounded by the urban heat island effect, or "UHI" effect, where built-up areas are warmer due to heat trapped by buildings and heat generated by activities, such as transportation and industry.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: To prepare for rising temperatures, the Government has adopted a science-based and proactive heat mitigation and adaption strategy, which has three prongs.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: First, we are deepening our understanding of the science behind how rising temperatures affects Singapore and our residents.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Second, we are reviewing efforts to strengthen the community's resilience to heat.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Third, we are designing effective heat mitigation strategies and scaling them up.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: First, understanding the science of how heat affects Singapore and our residents.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The CCRS translates global climate projections to understand the localised effects and implications for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This will enable our heat mitigation action plan and other climate adaptation planning to be informed by the latest IPCC findings and by local and regional warming trends.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: To understand how heat affects the Singapore population, we are driving research and development to study the factors contributing to urban heat, test different heat mitigation strategies and assess the effects of heat on public health.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: For example, under the Cooling Singapore 2.0 project, we are working with researchers to develop a digital model to simulate Singapore's urban climate and predict the effectiveness of various heat mitigation strategies.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This enables us to understand how heat affects different parts of Singapore and identify cost-effective heat mitigation strategies.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Second, we leverage science to design better policies and guidelines to strengthen community resilience to climate change, especially to account for the fact that some segments of our population, such as the elderly or outdoor workers, may be more vulnerable to rising temperatures.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: MOH and MSE are studying how heat stress could affect our population.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: MOH, MOM and the Workplace Safety and Health Council also work closely together to ensure that guidelines on managing heat stress at workplaces are regularly updated based on the latest scientific evidence, including the V3 study which I had earlier mentioned.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Third, designing effective heat mitigation strategies, of which there are two broad categories.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: First, measures to promote cooling in our urban environment, such as through urban planning and building guidelines, infusing more greenery and scaling up the use of cool materials on buildings.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Senior Minister of State Tan Kiat How will elaborate on these.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Second, measures to reduce the heat generated from human activities, such as from our homes, our roads and our industries.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: These include, for example, efforts under the Singapore Green Plan to electrify our vehicle population and to increase the energy efficiency of industrial, commercial and residential buildings.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Although Singapore has so far not faced heat crises on the same scale as other countries, it would not be possible to avoid the rise in temperatures due to global warming.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We must continue to engage and co-create solutions with the community to enhance our resilience to climate change.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will also roll out policies and measures to cool our neighbourhoods and community spaces, which Senior Minister of State Tan Kiat How will now elaborate on.
